 Business After the flood: Businesses wonder how they’ll survive El Niño
 The intense rain Wednesday could be the first test in a long, wet winter for city merchants.
 Total Wine on Harrison Street was one of several businesses that closed due to damage from flooding Wednesday. | Source: Courtesy Solve SF By George Kelly and Michael McLaughlin Published Nov. 19, 2026 at 3:37 p.m. Updated Nov. 20, 2026 at 9:26 a.m. Share Share

 Close share menu 1 There are 1 comments on this story Published Nov. 19, 2026 at 3:37 p.m. Updated Nov. 20, 2026 at 9:26 a.m. The photos made 14th Street in the Mission look like a lake Wednesday. Stagnant water formed pools several feet deep during the worst of the atmospheric river. But for a cluster of restaurants, the real damage came from inside. 
 Bageletto was one victim. Sewage gushed up through toilets, sinks, and floor drains, despite the owners’ $10,000 investment in floodgates.
 “The water wasn’t coming in from the doors. It was all coming in from the interior piping,” owner Kiki Theodorides said Thursday. She blamed San Francisco’s sewer infrastructure.
 ADVERTISEMENT
 Her husband, Rich D’Aloia, told staff to leave Wednesday after a toilet started spewing water, out of fear that someone could be electrocuted. The floodgates, which they bought weeks ago, held back the water outside.
 Still, the couple are looking at an expensive bill to reopen. “This is, like, a biohazard,” Theodorides said. They’ve contacted their insurer. The repairs will cost “thousands and thousands of dollars that we don’t have.”
 “We’re devastated,”  D’Aloia added.
 Neighboring businesses Pink Onion Pizza, the Rainbow Grocery, and Total Wine are in the same boat. They remained closed Thursday. Meanwhile, residents on the block hauled damaged furniture and belongings onto the sidewalk for removal.
 Similar scenes played out Wednesday across San Francisco as the severe storm left vast sections of the city submerged.

 EXCLUSIVE A pizzeria, a Yemeni cafe, snazzy storefronts: Inner Sunset gets the downtown treatment
 Devil’s Teeth Baking Company in the Outer Sunset closed early because Noriega Avenue was more like a fast-flowing canal than a navigable street. A dialysis center in the Mission canceled essential kidney treatments because its ground floor was pooled with water, according to a 311 complaint. At Hwa Mi Won restaurant on Geary Boulevard, workers used a wet vacuum to suck up water rising through drains in the bathroom, according to another complaint.
 The downpour dropped 2.64 inches of rain on San Francisco, equivalent to what the city gets in an average November, according to the National Weather Service. Storm drains became clogged with leaves and other debris, forming lagoons on busy boulevards and alleys. 
 A cleaning service van outside the closed Total Wine store Thursday. | Source: George Kelly/The Standard San Francisco is the only city on the West Coast that has a combined storm and wastewater system, so when the underground network of pipes gets overwhelmed by rainfall, the really gross stuff gets discharged into the ocean or finds its way into homes and businesses.
 On Thursday, the waters had receded, but many businesses spent the day cleaning up and making repairs, all while hoping to be spared from the next major storm.
 A plumber who inspected Bageletto said it would be nearly impossible to prevent a repeat, in part because building codes bar check valves in places, according to Theodorides. The problem could continue until the city fixes the underlying system, the plumber told her. 
 Property owners may be eligible for up to $100,000 in funding (opens in new tab) from the San Francisco Public Utilities Commission to pay for flood barriers, backflow prevention devices and drainage equipment.
 How bad was the flooding? It’s tough to quantify, but the Department of Public Works fielded 704 requests Wednesday to clear clogged catch basins. From Dec. 27, 2022, through Jan. 18, 2023 — another stretch of heavy rain in San Francisco — the department received 942 orders to deal with flooding and clogged storm drains.
 Furniture and debris cleared from a residence sits on a 14th Street sidewalk Thursday after flooding. | Source: George Kelly/The Standard Rintaro, a restaurant near Bageletto, closed Wednesday but was able to reopen Thursday. Some wine and sake got ruined, but damage was minimal, owner Sylvan Mishima Brackett said. 
 The day of lost business is painful, but nothing like what happened on Dec. 31, 2022, when two feet of water filled the interior. Staff preparing New Year’s bento boxes escaped through a window. Brackett estimated the total cost at $500,000 to $600,000. This summer, he installed floodgates, which he believes spared him this week from a replay.
 Brackett and Theodorides said Mayor Daniel Lurie and representatives of the Office of Small Business were planning to visit the neighborhood Thursday afternoon. The mayor’s office declined to confirm if the tour was on his schedule.
 “Our small businesses are incredibly resilient, but yesterday’s storms showed how quickly severe weather can disrupt daily operations and livelihoods,” said Katy Tang, director of the Office of Small Business. She urged merchants to document damage and make sure emergency plans are up to date. “As business owners begin to recover, it’s important to remember that more storms are expected in the coming days and throughout the winter.”
 A suited worker hoses down a metal grate outside Rainbow Grocery Coop on Thursday. | Source: George Kelly/The Standard Among bigger businesses, the story was different. Waymo halted service, then resumed Thursday morning, after its driverless electric cars appeared ill-equipped to maneuver around standing water.
 “More than a dozen” PG&E utility poles around the Bay Area were damaged, along with overhead wires, primarily due to falling branches and other vegetation, a spokesperson said. But the power outages that affected thousands of customers Wednesday had been reduced to fewer than 900 Thursday morning, the spokesperson said.
 Rain is in the forecast for the next week, with another powerful storm possible Tuesday and Wednesday that could be exacerbated by king tides. 
 “Do you clean, or do you just sit and wait?” Theodorides asked.
